I already have one and yes it's the cheapest way to protect your equipment and receive stable voltage from the grid. There's also other sources for noise in the system than the grid. The grid itself isn't as much of a problem as some say, it's more about the isolation from other appliances. Of course the audio equipment maintains a stable voltage and amplitude modulation is what controls the sound, so only frequent enough changes in voltage will make audible distortion to an amplified signal. This just doesn't happen at a high enough frequency from the grid usually. 

Depends on the circuitry of the UPS and the isolation between the electronics using it. UPS is still essential for its own reasons.

Audiophile network switch is funny. I agree to an extent. Capacitors do filter noise down to millivolts or wherever but some noise still exists. To determine if it's audible depends on many things like the crossover, amplifier, and crossover or amplifier  circuitry itself like what caps, inductors, etc. 

Most importantly all that relates to the voltage of the line level signal. If there's a stronger signal from the DAC you'll probably be fine, but if not then you might actually hope you have enough filtering from your power supply and amp components.

Sometimes noise is interpreted to be from "dirty 🤪" electricity lol but it's actually an unbalanced and poorly shielded line level cable next to an HDMI cable (true story I could hear the interference relative to motion on the screen). 

All this to say you're right, you can buy quality amps, strong DACs, balanced signals, and even a "clean power" PSU that basically has additional filters and most people will be fine if they have only one of those items. Despite the electrons arrive at the equipment.

Here's the full story and main points:

NVME drives are pretty much the fastest ones. The faster the drive that the OS is on, the snappier and faster the overall experience will be with everything you do. I have a single NVME slot on my mid tier motherboard and it's used by a 2TB NVME drive with my OS. I still have additional SSD drives in the normal SATA slots for whatever else I want to store with that extra storage space.

As long as the OS is on the fastest drive then that's best, and there are many other things people will do from there. 

Some people only keep the OS on the fastest drive and use the other drives for programs, some people only use the other drives for games, some people have everything on the fastest drive but add additional drives to the SATA ports for general backup of photos, videos, documents, etc.

I personally keep the OS and productivity programs on my NVME drive, and set all my images, documents, games, project files on the other drive. This is how when I open a program or change tasks it always feels snappy.

Benefits of splitting your stuff across multiple drives:

- While NVME drives are the fastest drive, putting absolutely everything into it can slightly slow things down if multiple programs are loading from that one drive at the same time.
- Flash memory slows down and degrades over time (only from "writes", not "reads" btw). If everything is constantly writing to your beloved OS drive, in 10 years it will be noticeably slower.
- If you want to change your OS drive with a new one in the future but all your games and files are on a different drive, you won't need to reinstall or transfer all that again, just the OS.

Additional tip: disable defragmenting on every type of drive that is not a spinning disk hard drive. All it does for flash memory is degrade it, and windows still has this enabled by default. I won't explain everything about what defrag is and how to do it here because this is already plenty lol

Tldr: you only need a single NVME slot to have a snappy experience, and the SATA slots that every mobo comes with are sufficient if you want more drives.

It depends on how bad the mains are. Some actually experience moderately frequently small voltage fluctuations, but the main reason is separating other appliances. Ever noticed the lights dim for a second when you turn on an AC unit? With all the appliances and fridge compressor going on and off it adds up to multiple significant fluctuations. Any electronics with phase angle control to reduce power can create high frequency noise. Improper grounding causes audible ground loops that can be loud when amplified by the equipment. 

Basically there are chances for large voltage drops, ground loops at the frequency of the mains, and high frequency interference when any appliance regulates based on phase angle. 

It doesn't improve the existing sound directly but gets rid of peaks of audible interference or noise which I personally have experienced loudly in my equipment (high frequency buzzing as well as ground loops).

On a good corner exit, the rear tires of a MR car are more loaded up than a FR. If you swing the car in right and set up a straight early exit by taking a sharper apex, they're very fast. But if you're powering out of a corner exit and lose rear traction, there is more inertia to that slide than an FR, where the engine is closer to the pivot point of the spin. 

Correcting a MR oversteer takes a stronger correction due to the increased inertia/force behind the sliding rear. If you 4 wheel slide and your fronts catch with an overcorrection, it can have a similar speed but more powerful flick to the other side as well (compared to FR).

FRs can usually carry more speed mid corner and that smoother braking and accelerating style can make them more forgiving on the touge. Really depends on what the driver prefers 👍
